sections.heading: Longing to be what pleases you
sections.text: My God, it feels like a taste of heaven simply to please you and to become the person you want me to be. I want to be holy because you are holy. I want the purity of Christ to shape me. I want your Spirit to make me whole and mature in every part of me. Your commands are not a burden to me; they are beautiful. So why do I keep resisting them? Why do I still break what I know is good?
theological_themes: God’s holiness as the standard and desire of the believer
Longing for sanctification and moral purity

scripture_references.connection: Peter calls Christians to holiness because God himself is holy, grounding the believer’s moral life in God’s own character rather than in mere rule-keeping.
John teaches that love for God changes how his commandments are viewed; they are not meant to be hated burdens but the path of loving obedience.

sections.heading: Grieving that I sin against such kindness
sections.text: I am deeply sorry that I am still a sinner, and that my sin grieves you—the God who has shown me nothing but goodness, mercy, and grace. If you only punished me, that would be terrible; but what cuts me even deeper is that I offend you while you keep answering me with kindness. I sin again and again, and still you do not stop being patient and generous toward me.
theological_themes: God’s patience and kindness toward sinners
Grieving God rather than treating sin lightly

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, showing that sin is not merely rule-breaking but a personal offense against the God who has sealed his people.
Paul says God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance; this supports the prayer’s grief that divine mercy, not only judgment, exposes the ugliness of sin.

sections.heading: Wanting my life to honor you
sections.text: At times I think I could endure almost any suffering if only I did not dishonor you. How can I treat lightly the glory of the God who is so good? Teach me what it means, today and every day, to glorify you and worship you with my actual life—not only with my words.
theological_themes: Desire to honor God above comfort

scripture_references.connection: Paul applies God’s glory to ordinary actions, showing that worship is not limited to formal religious moments but includes the whole shape of daily life.
Paul presents the believer’s body and life as a living sacrifice, which directly supports the prayer’s desire for practical, embodied worship.

sections.heading: Giving myself wholly to you
sections.text: I want to hand over my whole self to you—my soul, my body, my plans, my time, my desires, without holding anything back. Keep me from trying to belong to myself. Bend my will toward yours. Train my loves until they agree with your love. I do not want a private corner of my heart where I still insist on being my own master.
theological_themes: Consecration of the whole person to God
Belonging to God rather than self

scripture_references.connection: Paul reminds believers that they are not their own because they were bought with a price, grounding the prayer’s desire to stop claiming ownership over oneself.
Paul describes Christian life as no longer centered on the self but lived by faith in Christ, which fits the prayer’s longing to have the will and life reshaped by God.

sections.heading: Joining the worship you deserve
sections.text: And yet, Lord, I know I still cannot live in this world without sin. I hate that reality, and I do not want to make peace with it. Let the angels praise you without stopping. Let all heaven bow low before you, the blessed King. I long to join their worship, now and forever. But even if I praised you for all eternity, I would still only be giving you a tiny part of the honor you deserve. So please give me a heart filled with your own heavenly love—love that worships you gladly and belongs to you completely.
theological_themes: Need for divine love to fill the heart

scripture_references.connection: John refuses the claim that believers are already without sin, while also directing them to honest confession and God’s faithful forgiveness.
John’s vision of countless heavenly beings worshiping the Lamb gives biblical shape to the prayer’s longing to join the angels in unending praise.
Paul says God’s love is poured into believers’ hearts through the Holy Spirit, supporting the final request for a heart filled with divine love.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly laments the believer’s continuing sin and asks whether sin is in some sense unavoidable in this life. That touches debated Christian discussions about remaining sin, perfection, and sanctification. The adaptation preserves the lament without turning it into an excuse or a denial of growth in holiness.

The original uses angelic worship and prostration as an image of fitting humility before God. The adaptation keeps the heavenly-worship theme without implying that human worship must copy a specific physical posture.
significant_interpretive_choices: The line about God’s punishment not wounding as deeply as offending his kindness was rendered as grief over sinning against mercy, not as minimizing judgment. The point is that love and grace make sin feel more grievous to the believer.
The wish to have no will or affections outside God’s will was interpreted as wholehearted surrender and rightly ordered love, not the loss of personality or agency.
The final request for a heart full of divine, heavenly love was rendered as a request for God-given love that fuels worship and consecration, rather than as a vague emotional experience.
